title: 'Haunted History,' 'Young Frankenstein' kick off Halloween in St. Paul and Stillwater
excerpt: Festivities kick off with a presentation by the Twin Cities Paranormal Society — and a production of “Young Frankenstein” that’s not so young.
content:
As grocery store aisles teem with black-and-orange editions of supersized candy bundles and everything from your coffee shop to your office lobby leaves a lingering pumpkin flavor, “spooky season” reaches a fever pitch this month.

Those looking for an alternative to celebrating Halloween with bars — candy or dive — can partake in the holiday spirit with some more dramatic events starting this weekend.

In Stillwater, a deep dive into history and haunting

The Warden’s House Museum in Stillwater will hold a paranormal event in partnership with the Washington County Historical Society.

The Twin Cities Paranormal Society will present findings from a recent investigation at the house, which, according to the Washington County Historical Society, was home to 13 different wardens over 61 years, until the prison moved to Bayport in 1914. The museum opened in 1941 after the Historical Society acquired the property from the state of Minnesota.

“Haunted History at the Warden’s House: Afterlife Sentences” will be presented in two shows per night, beginning at 6 and 8 p.m., Friday and Saturday, Oct. 2 and 3.

Heidi Heinze, museum site manager for the Warden’s House, said the paranormal investigators follow a methodology that works alongside scientific reasoning.

“I know they work hard to kind of debunk any possible evidence that they might find,” Heinze said. “So what ends up coming through in the presentation is pretty authentic stuff that I don’t think can be manipulated or fooled with. If you come and hear some of these voices — and the audio that they capture — it’s pretty incredible.”

The Twin Cities Paranormal Society turns 20 this year. Thomas Kingsley Troupe, children’s author and lead investigator, said each investigator is background-checked.

The team, including a salesman, a high school teacher, a retiree and a 911 operator — all have day jobs. Troupe said they dedicate hours or days outside of the investigations themselves — which can eat up multiple nights — to review footage and captures.

Troupe said they don’t function like ghost-hunting programming. They’re a nonprofit organization whose operations continue independent of viewership. After the lengthy rule-out process is completed — then paranormal activity is ruled as a possibility.

“We always say, here are the things we found that we can’t explain,” Troupe said.

A not-so-young Frankenstein takes the stage in St. Paul

Theatre 55 will present a production of “Young Frankenstein” — a musical adaptation of Mel Brooks’ film of the same name — staged entirely by actors aged 55 and older, who will perform at St. Paul’s Gremlin Theatre from Oct. 9-25. The show follows Dr. Frankenstein’s grandson as he travels to Transylvania to claim his family’s castle and reanimate the dead.

Richard Hitchler, founder and artistic director of Theatre 55, started the troupe to highlight the underutilized talent of older actors.

“I hear about theaters with their concerns about getting a younger audience, and bringing the younger audience in — and my thought is, why fight that?” Hitchler said. “We have plenty of seniors with an immense amount of talent.”

Hitchler said “Young Frankenstein” is a production best performed by an older ensemble, in that Brooks’ comedy relies on a style of subtlety and timing not often understood by younger dramatists.

“I saw a production of this done by a group of younger people, and they just missed all the timing — and all the understanding of what Mel Brooks was getting at,” Hitchler said. “Mel Brooks himself is 100 years old this year, so he has a certain type of vaudevillian humor.”
